current_episode.title: Hot Dam: Why beavers are Britain’s new climate heroes

guest.bio_context: Lauren Frayer is an NPR reporter who traveled to multiple locations across Britain — including Napdale Forest in western Scotland and the Ealing Beaver Project in West London — to report on the reintroduction of beavers as a climate adaptation strategy. She visited four different beaver locations, hiked with forest rangers at 4 a.m., and interviewed scientists, veterinarians, farmers, and conservationists for this investigation.

context.real_quote: The beavers can do it, probably a fraction of the cost, probably better than we can, certainly more sustainably for the environment.
key_stats: 1992: EU law passed requiring member states to investigate extinct species caused by human activity and explore reintroduction — the legal trigger for Britain's beaver reintroduction program
Early 20th century: beavers hunted to extinction in Britain; only approximately 1,200 beavers remained across Europe and northern Asia at that point
2009: first two Norwegian beavers, Millie and Bjornar, relocated to Napdale Forest in western Scotland
Flood mitigation engineering costs at the London tube station site estimated at hundreds of thousands to over one million pounds — replaced by beaver-led solution at a fraction of that cost
Ealing Beaver Project, West London: 8 new bird species and 2 new bat species recorded since beavers arrived, with bat count rising from 4 to 6 species
20-acre park adjacent to the London tube station where beavers were relocated — formerly a golf course — transformed into a water-retaining wetland within weeks of beaver arrival

pending_qa.q: What are 'beaver bombers' and why are they causing controversy in Scotland?
pending_qa.r: Beaver bombers are renegade wildlife enthusiasts who illegally release unlicensed beavers into areas — particularly large farming zones in Scotland — where they were not officially placed, in order to speed up rewilding. The practice is illegal and has intensified conflict between conservationists and farmers, with some farmers responding by illegally shooting beavers that appear on their land.

pending_qa.q: How are beavers being used to fight wildfires in the United States?
pending_qa.r: Beavers have been released into fire-damaged areas of Washington state following wildfires across the American West. Research has found that areas with beavers retain more water and are therefore more resilient to fire, making beaver reintroduction an emerging tool in wildfire mitigation strategy.

pending_qa.q: Why do beavers build dams even in Britain where their natural predators no longer exist?
pending_qa.r: Beavers build dams instinctively to raise water levels so they can hide underwater from predators such as wolves and bears. Even though all of those predators have gone extinct in Britain, beavers continue to build dams because they have no way of knowing that the threat no longer exists — their behavior is hard-wired rather than learned.

pending_qa.q: What is castoreum and how was it historically used?
pending_qa.r: Castoreum is an anal secretion produced by beavers, used historically as a scent marker similar to how dogs mark territory. In medieval times it was used in perfumes for its vanilla-like scent, and Romans consumed it as a form of aspirin, believing it had medicinal properties. The demand for castoreum, alongside beaver fur and meat, contributed to the species' extinction in Britain by the early 20th century.
